title: One Buddha or many
hookLine: the historical Buddha, and the many Buddhas of the Mahayana

lines: A KYOTO ALTAR: A SKY OF BUDDHAS.
cards: Two altars. On the first, in a village temple in Sri Lanka, one seated figure: a man who walked the dusty roads of northern India, ate what was put in his bowl, grew old, fell ill, and died among his friends.

On the second, in a temple in Kyoto, a golden Buddha with his hand raised, and behind him a painted sky crowded with more Buddhas than anyone could count, each with a world of its own. Same word on both altars: Buddha.
Two pictures of who that is, and how many.

teach.h: GOTAMA: ONE TEACHER, AN OLD CART.
teach.b: First, the one. In the Pali texts, the Buddha of our age is Gotama: a teacher with a body that aches, who tells Ananda near the end that he is like an old cart held together with straps.
His last words, in Rhys Davids's translation, are plain and human: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!"
The Theravada honors that one teacher, gone into final nibbana, and the teaching that remains. Second, even the Pali texts look backward and forward.
A long discourse names Buddhas who came before Gotama, in ages long past, and another speaks of Metteyya, a Buddha still to come. One Buddha for an age; many across time. Third, the many.
Mahayana sutras widen the picture into space.
Amitabha, the Buddha of boundless light, presides over a pure land in the west, and Pure Land Buddhists call on his name. The Medicine Buddha heals in a land of lapis light.
Vairocana shines at the center of the cosmos in Japanese and Chinese temples.

And the Lotus Sutra adds a startling turn: the Buddha who seemed to be born, awaken and die, it says, actually awakened ages beyond measure ago, and showed a death as a teaching device so people would not grow careless.

Fourth, how each holds it. For the Theravada, honoring one teacher who truly walked and truly died is the heart of devotion. For the Mahayana schools that hold it, the vast picture shows how wide awakening is.

how: Theravada Buddhists honor Gotama, the Buddha of this age, at temple and home shrines, while Mahayana Buddhists also honor other Buddhas, such as Amitabha in Pure Land practice and the Medicine Buddha.

games.q: what does “one buddha or many” mean?
o: whether the Buddha was one real man or a legend of many men
how many statues a temple may place on its main altar
whether there is one Buddha of our age or Buddhas beyond count

games.q: one and many: tap the pairs.
p: boundless light, a pure land in the west
an old cart held with straps
the Buddha's picture of his aging body

s: the Pali texts know of only one Buddha, ever
they name Buddhas before Gotama and Metteyya still to come.
Amitabha is another name for the historical Buddha
in Pure Land sutras, Amitabha is a different Buddha, of boundless light, in a western land.
the Lotus Sutra says the Buddha awakened ages beyond measure ago
it presents his death as a teaching device, so people would not grow careless.

games.q: you're at a Kyoto temple, looking at a painted sky full of Buddhas. a friend from a Sri Lankan temple asks: so which is it, one or many?
o: many; the one is just a starting point.
each school explains its own picture: one for an age, many across time and space.
games.why: even the Pali texts speak of Buddhas before and after Gotama; the Mahayana widens the picture. each altar is explained in its own home.

practice: First picture the one: an old man walking slowly on a dusty road, his robe faded, his friends around him. Then let the picture open, like a camera pulling back to the night sky, light upon light, world upon world.
You don't need to choose; let each be what it is for those who hold it.

wordCard.voice: One Buddha or many. The Buddha of our age, Gotama, honored as one teacher who lived and died; and the many Buddhas across time and space in the Mahayana. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit buddha: awakened, one who has woken up.

carryVoice: Your line: one and many. Each school explains its own altar. Go gently.
